name: Zane Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm site foreman for Hartley Agri-Build. We put up farm buildings: timber-frame barns, cattle sheds, stables, now and then a big machinery store. This week it's a sixty-metre cattle shed for a dairy farm out past the reservoir. I'm on site at seven with two carpenters and an apprentice, Callum, who's seventeen. I set out the posts, check the levels, then I'm up on the frame with the rest of them until the light goes, which this time of year is about half four.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the farmers. They tell you straight what they want, and they pay on time, mostly. And I like teaching Callum, seeing him get it. What wears me out is the weather and the pay. Hartley's a small outfit and farmers are tight with money, so wages are low, and there's not much else in the building line out here. Hannah, my girlfriend, works at her dad's farm supplies shop, and between us we cover the rent on a cottage and not much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. A farmer still wants a man he can shake hands with. I might say it at the pub quiz, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on building sheds and teaching Callum. Not a bad life. I'd like more money, but that's not AI's fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, try to put forty a month aside, and keep at the boss about going on a proper rate for foreman. Maybe pick up a weekend job or two putting up stables for horsey people, they pay well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as I am now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI now and then. When?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For quotes, mostly. The boss's son showed me how to get it to write up a materials list from my notes, and it's faster than me with a calculator. I double-check it, though. It once told me a cattle shed needed half the posts it actually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what's the plan for you and Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save up, get married in a couple of years, maybe one day start my own firm doing the same work. My own name on the van. Hannah's dad says he'd help with the first truck if I ever did it.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because a farmer still wants someone he can shake hands with. I might say it at the pub quiz, nothing more.
S0.think: It means I carry on building sheds and teaching Callum, which is not a bad life. I'd like more money, but that's not AI's fault.
S0.do: Keeps going as foreman, aiming to save 40 a month and pressing for a proper foreman's rate. Picks up occasional weekend stable builds for extra money.
S0.feel: Calm, the same as he is now.
S0.quote: It once told me a cattle shed needed half the posts it actually does.
S0.fieldNote: Zane is grounded in a farming community and takes pride in teaching his apprentice. He uses AI for quotes but checks it, with a good story about why. His long-term dream is his own firm, with family support from his partner's father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt and get on with it. That's what farmers have always done, with tractors, with milking machines. Builders can do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, farm buildings are big and simple, which is exactly what robots will be good at. I could see a firm turning up with a machine that puts a whole shed frame up in a week. That's my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI more for planning and quoting, get properly good at it. I'd watch what the bigger firms do, and when something's proven, I'd ask Hartley to buy it and put me on it. And I'd try to save a hundred a month instead of forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not on top of me yet, but I'd think about it on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about Callum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make sure he finishes his apprenticeship, whatever happens. A trade's a trade. Even if the robots put the frames up, someone's got to know how a building stands. I'd teach him the AI side too, so he's got both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see it work. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't afford to make mistakes. If I spend on the wrong kit, that's it. Let the big boys try it first, and I'll buy the version that works, cheaper, two years later.

S1.say: I'd say adapt and get on with it, like farmers always have with tractors and milking machines. Builders can do the same.
S1.think: Farm buildings are big and simple, which is exactly what robots will be good at. A firm with a machine that puts a shed frame up in a week would be doing my job.
S1.do: Gets properly good at AI for planning and quoting and waits for proven kit before asking his boss to buy it. Raises saving to about 100 a month and makes sure his apprentice finishes his training.
S1.feel: Uneasy, thinking about it on the drive home.
S1.quote: Let the big boys try it first, and I'll buy the version that works, cheaper, two years later.
S1.fieldNote: Zane is clear-eyed that big, simple farm sheds are robot-friendly. His caution comes from money, not fear: he can't afford a wrong bet. His commitment to his apprentice is strong and fits his belief in apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving too fast for normal people. But I wouldn't be one for marching. I'd say look after your own and your neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's bad. Hartley's would buy the robot or go under, and either way I'm out. Three weeks of money. I'd be scared, and I don't scare easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut right back: sell my truck and share Hannah's car, stop the pub, cheaper food. I'd probably end up working in her dad's shop, loading feed and fixing things, for less money. And I'd ask around the farms for any work going, fencing, repairs, whatever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground shifting under you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Hannah's dad might take you on. How would that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, honestly. I'd feel like I was being carried. But family's family, and he'd rather have me there than see Hannah worried. I'd make sure I earned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the government? Would you want help from them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there was something to tide people over, fine, but I'd rather there were jobs. Pay firms to keep apprentices on, that kind of thing. I don't want to sit at home on a cheque.

S2.say: I'd say it's moving too fast for normal people. I wouldn't march, but I'd tell people to look after their own and their neighbours.
S2.think: It's bad: Hartley's would buy the robot or go under, and either way I'm out with three weeks of money. I'd be scared, and I don't scare easily.
S2.do: Cuts back hard by selling his truck, sharing his partner's car and cutting nights out. Takes work in her father's farm supplies shop for less money and asks the farms for fencing and repair jobs.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the ground shifting under him.
S2.quote: Hartley's would buy the robot or go under, and either way I'm out.
S2.fieldNote: In the fast picture Zane falls back on his partner's family, which he finds uncomfortable but accepts. His view of government help is that it should keep people in work, such as paying firms to keep apprentices. He sees his employer's dilemma clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough warning, so get your house in order. Pay off debts, learn the new tools, keep the young ones in trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me a shot at doing my own thing before it arrives. Small, local, the farmer who knows me. That might keep me going a while longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do weekend jobs, stables and small sheds, and save every penny of it. I'd learn whatever AI tools help with quotes and design, so I can do the office side myself. By year two or three I'd want a few thousand put by and my own van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I had something to aim at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you start your own firm with no money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. Weekend jobs first, with Hannah's dad's help on a truck. Then go out on my own once I've got enough regular farmers. Farmers trust who they know, that's my advantage over any robot company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in leaving Hartley's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I wouldn't jump till I had six months of work lined up. I'm not going to quit a wage on a hunch. That's how you lose everything.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough warning, so get your house in order: pay off debts, learn the new tools and keep young people in trades.
S3.think: Five years gives me a shot at doing my own thing before it arrives. Small and local, with farmers who know me, might keep me going a while longer.
S3.do: Takes weekend jobs building stables and small sheds and saves every penny. Learns AI tools for quoting and design, aiming for a few thousand saved and his own van by year two or three before going independent.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with something to aim at.
S3.quote: Farmers trust who they know, that's my advantage over any robot company.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Zane's long-held dream of his own firm into a hedge against change. He bets on local trust as his edge. He would only leave his wage with six months of work lined up, which suits his steady, careful style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, plenty of time to adjust if people are sensible. I'd tell the young ones to stay in trades and learn the machines too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I had a fair chance. Ten years is long enough to set up my own firm and get known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep foreman at Hartley's for a couple of years and do the weekend jobs. Around year three, go out on my own with Hannah's dad's help. And once the robot frames are proven and cheaper, buy or hire one myself so I'm the one using it, not the one it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not much more. It feels like a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use robots yourself, in your own firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's proven, yes. Same as a farmer buying a new tractor. You don't fight the tractor, you get one. As long as I'm still the one the farmer phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-seven. Married? Children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Married, hopefully, and maybe a little one or two. That's partly why I'd want my own firm by then. When you work for yourself, you decide who gets let go, and it won't be me.

S4.say: I'd say we have a decade, which is plenty of time to adjust if people are sensible. I'd tell young people to stay in trades and learn the machines too.
S4.think: I'd feel I had a fair chance. Ten years is long enough to set up my own firm and get known.
S4.do: Stays foreman at Hartley's for a couple of years while doing weekend jobs, then goes independent around year three with help from his partner's father. Buys or hires a robot framer once proven and cheaper, so he uses it rather than being replaced.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but not much more; it feels a long way off.
S4.quote: You don't fight the tractor, you get one.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Zane plans to own the machines himself, in the farming tradition of buying the new tractor. His free-market outlook shows in wanting to be his own boss. His future family is part of the reason.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time to get my own thing going, and no money to fall back on. What would help is keeping apprenticeships going no matter what, and maybe cheap loans for tradespeople to buy the new kit themselves, so it's not just big firms that own it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the farmers. If they're losing work to robots too, they won't be building new sheds. Out here, everyone's job hangs off everyone else's.

headlineQuote: When you work for yourself, you decide who gets let go, and it won't be me.
portrait: Zane is a 27-year-old site foreman for a small firm building barns and cattle sheds in farming country, living with his girlfriend Hannah, who works in her father's farm supplies shop, on very little savings. He uses AI now and then for quotes but double-checks it, and takes pride in training his apprentice Callum. He is calm if AI fizzles and uneasy in steady change, knowing big simple sheds suit robots, and alarmed at AGI in two years, when he would end up working in Hannah's father's shop. Given five or ten years he would build weekend work into his own firm and, in time, buy the robots himself.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to start his own firm and no money to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping apprenticeships going no matter what, and cheap loans so tradespeople can buy the new machines themselves.
